hooks: The Highland line is a real geological boundary, the Highland Boundary Fault, and the name marks a cultural border as much as a physical one.
Gaelic survives here more than anywhere: in the Western Isles about half the population still speaks it.
Ben Nevis at 1,345 m is Britain's highest point, and the Highland Clearances emptied these glens of people for sheep between 1750 and 1860.
Eurostat's name for Scotland's north-east — the land the old earldom of Mar and the city of Aberdeen sit in.
Aberdeen is the granite city, built almost entirely from stone quarried at Rubislaw, once the biggest man-made hole in Europe.
North Sea oil came ashore here from 1975 and turned a fishing port into Europe's offshore capital.
Scotland's eastern belt, holding Edinburgh and the old kingdom of Fife — Fife is one of the oldest place names in Scotland, from a Pictish district.
Edinburgh's old and new towns are together a UNESCO site, the new one laid out in 1767 on a grid while the old climbs the volcanic ridge.
The Forth Bridge of 1890 was the first big steel structure in Britain, and painting it became a proverb for a job never finished.
Scotland's south-west and industrial middle, centred on Glasgow — whose name is Brittonic glas cau, "green hollow".
Clyde shipyards built a fifth of the world's ships by 1900, including the Queen Mary and the QE2.
Burns was born at Alloway in Ayrshire here, and his birthday is marked with a supper worldwide.
This was Northumbria, the "land north of the Humber" — a kingdom that once reached from the Humber to Edinburgh.
Hadrian's Wall crosses it, 117 km built from AD 122, and Newcastle's name is from a castle of 1080 that was new then.
Lindisfarne off its coast produced the Lindisfarne Gospels around 700 and was the first place the Vikings raided in 793.
Lancashire and Cumbria — Cumbria is from the same root as Cymru, the Welsh name for Wales, because Brittonic was spoken here longest.
Manchester was the first industrial city in the world, and cotton made it; Liverpool shipped the cotton and, earlier, the slaves who grew it.
The Lake District in it is England's largest national park, and Wordsworth and Beatrix Potter both made it famous.
York is Norse Jórvík, itself from Roman Eboracum, probably "place of the yews"; the Humber is an older, pre-English river name nobody has explained.
Yorkshire was the largest English county and was split in Ridings — from Norse thriðjungr, a third, which is why there were three and no South Riding.
York was the Viking capital of England for nearly a century, and its street names still end in -gate, Norse for a street.
The Midlands is simply the middle land of England, and this half was the core of Mercia, the kingdom that dominated the 700s.
The Danelaw's Five Boroughs — Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham and Stamford — were all here, which is why the dialect is full of Norse words.
Sherwood Forest and the Robin Hood story belong to it, and so does Melton Mowbray's pork pie, which has protected status.
The other half of Mercia, and the Black Country in it was named for the soot and the thirty-foot coal seam beneath it.
Birmingham had more canal miles than Venice at its peak, built to move coal and iron.
Shakespeare was born at Stratford-upon-Avon here, and the Industrial Revolution's first iron bridge was cast just over its edge at Coalbrookdale.
The English called them Wealas, "foreigners"; the Welsh call the country Cymru, "fellow countrymen" — two names for the same people from opposite sides.
Cardiff was the world's largest coal port by 1913, shipping what the valleys dug.
Offa's Dyke, an earthwork 8th-century Mercia built along this border, is still walkable for 285 km.
The Valleys are the narrow coal valleys of the south; west Wales is where Welsh is strongest, over half the population in Gwynedd and Anglesey.
Wales had over 600 working pits in 1913 and none by 1995; the last, Tower Colliery, was bought and run by its own miners.
Snowdonia is here, and the slate landscape of north-west Wales — which roofed the nineteenth-century world — is a UNESCO site.
East Anglia, the land of the East Angles, one of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms — the Angles are also where England got its name.
The Fens were drained by Dutch engineers from the 1630s and are the flattest, most fertile land in Britain, some of it below sea level.
Sutton Hoo in Suffolk held a ship burial of about 625, probably a king's, with a helmet that is now the emblem of the period.
Londinium is pre-Roman and unexplained — the best guess is a Brittonic name meaning something like the place at the unfordable river.
It was the largest city in the world from about 1825 to 1925, and about 300 languages are spoken in it today.
The 1666 fire destroyed 13,200 houses and 87 churches, and Wren rebuilt 51 of them plus St Paul's.
Kent is the oldest recorded place name in Britain, written by Pytheas around 325 BC; Sussex and Essex are the South and East Saxons.
The Channel is 33 km wide at Dover, and the tunnel under it, opened in 1994, has the longest undersea section of any rail tunnel.
Canterbury has been the seat of English Christianity since 597, and Chaucer's pilgrims were walking there.
Cornwall is Kernow plus the same wealas, "foreigners" — literally the foreigners of Kernow; Devon is from the Dumnonii tribe.
Cornish died out as an everyday language around 1800 and has been revived since; the county was tin country for 4,000 years.
Stonehenge and Bath are both here: the stones were raised around 2500 BC, and Bath's spring has poured 46 °C water since long before Rome plumbed it.
